title: Anas ibn Malik
hookLine: served the Prophet ten years and never once heard him ask, why did you do that

cards: A boy is sent on an errand. He says out loud that he won't go, though inside he means to. On the way through the market he comes upon some children playing, and there he stops.
The errand waits. Then a hand takes him gently by the back of the neck. He looks up, and the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is laughing.
Little Anas, did you go where I asked you? Yes, says the boy, I'm going now. Sahih Muslim keeps the scene, told by the boy himself.
Today: the servant who was never scolded.

teach.b: Anas ibn Malik came into the Prophet's household as a boy. Bukhari records his mother, Umm Sulaym, saying to the Prophet: Anas is your servant; pray for him. And the Prophet did.

Years later Anas summed up that house in one sentence that both Bukhari and Muslim keep. I served the Prophet for ten years, and he never said to me so much as uff. Never, about something I had done, why did you do that?
Never, about something I had left undone, why didn't you do that? Ten years of jobs in a busy household. Some done badly, some forgotten, some put off while a boy stopped among children at play.
Anas doesn't say he was perfect. He says he was never made to answer for it with a sharp word. And notice the word he picks: uff.
Not a lecture or a punishment, just the smallest sigh of annoyance, the noise people make before they even think.
The Qur'an uses that same little word in the surah called the Night Journey, telling believers not to say uff to aging parents.

teach.h: NEVER: WHY DID YOU DO THAT?
teach.b: Anas reports he never heard even that much. Some teachers cite this hadith on the Prophet's character, and on how to treat anyone who works for you or under you: children, students, staff.
Ten years of small failures, met with patience.

how: Muslims often cite Anas's report of ten years without a harsh word when teaching about the Prophet's character and about kindness to children, students and anyone who works for them.

o: a formal complaint made to the head of a house
a sharp lecture after a job is done badly
the smallest sigh of annoyance, before a word

games.q: Anas ibn Malik — tap the pairs.
p: brought her son and asked for a prayer

s: Anas said he never made mistakes in the Prophet's house
he says the opposite: things done and left undone, and never a 'why did you do that?'
the Prophet found Anas among children in the market instead of on his errand, and laughed
Anas tells it in Sahih Muslim: a hand on the back of his neck, and laughter.
Anas came to the Prophet as a grown man
his mother Umm Sulaym offered him as the Prophet's servant and asked for a prayer, and Muslim's report finds him among children in the market.

games.q: you're the Prophet. the boy you sent on an errand has stopped among children playing in the market. what do you do?
o: scold him in front of the other children.
take him by the neck, laughing, and ask if he went.
send someone else and say nothing.
games.why: Anas says he looked up and the Prophet was laughing: did you go where I asked? yes, I'm going.

practice: Think of the person you're most likely to snap at, and the small thing they might get wrong: the late reply, the dish left out, the job half done.

Picture that moment, and let the uff go out with your breath before it reaches your mouth; then choose what you'd say instead, a question, a joke, or nothing at all. If you pray, you can ask for patience with that one person.

wordCard.voice: Uff, the smallest sigh of annoyance, the word Anas ibn Malik said he never heard in ten years serving the Prophet's house. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the smallest sound of annoyance, the word Anas says he never heard.

carryVoice: Your line: ten years, no scolding. Not even the smallest sigh. Day eight hundred thirty-eight, done.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 2309 / Sahih al-Bukhari 6038 (ten years, never uff, never why did you do that)
